title: Ang 929–938: the Oankar
tomorrow: yogis on a mountain ask Nanak: who's your guru? he says…

cards: Small kids learning their letters get a song, sung until it sticks. Ang 929 begins a poem built the same way. Dakhni Oankar: Guru Nanak, in Ramkali, walking through the letters one by one.
Tradition places it in the south, among pandits, teachers of reading and writing, and the poem itself turns to a teacher with a writing board and speaks to him.
Underneath it sits one question: what is all this reading and writing for?

teach.b: It opens on the first sound. In paraphrase: from Oankar, the One, even Brahma came forth. Then letter by letter, each sound becomes a door.
And in the middle, the poem turns to the teacher.
In paraphrase: listen, teacher, why write about tangles? Write the Name of the Lord. So that's the answer: reading is for finding the One who wrote you.
The alphabet is a ladder, not the roof.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: PSALM 119, A TO Z.
teach.b: Here's a neighbor who did something close. In the Hebrew Bible, Psalm 119 is built on the Hebrew alphabet, each section headed by its letter, aleph, beth, all the way through.
And it says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society version: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, And a light unto my path."
Two traditions, two alphabets, and one shared instinct: teach what matters most through the very letters children learn first. And one honest difference.
Psalm 119 sings its love for God's teaching given in the Torah: its statutes, its commandments, words to be kept and walked in.
Oankar points the reader past the letters toward the Name and the Guru's word. Both love the page. Each loves it for its own reason, in its own words, and neither has to become the other to be true.

how: Dakhni Oankar is read and sung in Ramkali; some Sikh teachers use it to walk children through the Gurmukhi letters along with their meanings.

games.why: a real shared instinct, teaching through letters, and an honest difference in what each loves: the Torah's teaching, or the Name and the Guru's word.

practice: Look at one letter on a page near you, any letter, in any alphabet, for the whole sit. See it the way a child does the first time: the curve, the line, the small space inside it.
If you can, open to ang 929 and let your eyes rest on the poem's first letter.
